title: Climate hazards are becoming an education-disruption pathway that concentrates learning and lifetime-earnings risks in lower-income countries
source_unit: UNICEF, Learning Interrupted: Global Snapshot on Climate-related School Disruptions in 2025
geography: Global analysis of climate-related school disruption from pre-primary through upper-secondary education across 106 countries and territories

denominator.unit: countries and territories with schools affected by climate hazards in UNICEF's 2025 analysis

students_affected.unit: students from pre-primary through upper-secondary education experiencing school disruption due to climate events in 2025, at least

share_students_affected.unit: at least percent of students whose schooling was disrupted by climate-related hazards in 2025

lower_income_country_share.unit: percent of affected students living in low- and lower-middle-income countries

countries_multiple_events.unit: countries experiencing multiple climate-related school-disruption events in 2025

observations.method: UNICEF global snapshot linking climate-hazard events and education disruption across pre-primary, primary, lower-secondary, and upper-secondary schooling.
observations.uncertainty: The estimate captures reported or identified disruption and likely undercounts unreported, partial, informal, or indirect interruptions; duration, severity, school quality, and student-level learning loss vary.
observations.subgroup: Students, schools, teachers, families, and education systems in countries with different hazard exposure, income levels, infrastructure, adaptation capacity, and repeated events.
observations.counterinterpretation: Not every closure produces lasting learning loss; resilient schools, remote learning, catch-up programmes, safe transport, and rapid recovery can limit duration and damage, though access to those responses is unequal.

observations.period: 2025; climate-related learning disruption and economic trajectory

denominator.unit: students identified as affected by climate-related school disruption in 2025

lifetime_earnings_risk.unit: US dollars in estimated lifetime earnings potentially lost through disrupted learning and widening education inequalities

education_equity_pathway.value: climate disruption can widen existing education inequalities
education_equity_pathway.unit: reported pathway from hazard exposure to learning and future opportunity

repeated_disruption.unit: reported persistence pattern that can prevent recovery between shocks

observations.method: UNICEF synthesis connecting school-disruption estimates to learning, education inequality, and modeled lifetime-earnings implications.
observations.uncertainty: The earnings estimate is modeled and depends on assumptions about lost learning, schooling duration, future wages, recovery, and labour markets; it is not an observed individual earnings loss.
observations.subgroup: Children in lower-income countries, students with limited remote-learning access, girls, children with disabilities, displaced children, teachers, and households absorbing repeated school interruption.
observations.counterinterpretation: Climate investment in resilient infrastructure, continuity plans, accessible technology, teacher support, and social protection can reduce both learning and economic losses.

continuity_requirements.value: climate-resilient school infrastructure, early warning, disaster preparedness, safe access, flexible delivery, and recovery support
continuity_requirements.unit: institutional response routes implied by the report's disruption pathway

distributional_concentration.value: higher disruption burden in low- and lower-middle-income countries

cultural_continuity.value: school disruption interrupts learning, routines, peer relationships, protection, and pathways into work

observations.method: UNICEF interpretation of climate hazards as education-system, child-rights, social-protection, and future-opportunity risks.
observations.uncertainty: The report identifies system mechanisms and priority responses but does not evaluate every adaptation intervention or establish a universal causal effect on social cohesion, work, or political participation.
observations.subgroup: Education ministries, schools, teachers, children, families, local governments, climate-adaptation agencies, humanitarian actors, and communities in hazard-prone places.
observations.counterinterpretation: Education systems can become resilience infrastructure when they remain safe, accessible, and locally responsive during crises; disruption is not an inevitable endpoint of climate exposure.

related_sources.claim: UNICEF flagship-report context on global trends affecting children.

boundary: This record adds a climate-hazard-to-school-continuity, learning, lifetime-opportunity, public-infrastructure, and social-continuity route. It is not student-level attendance, learning assessment, household adaptation, or individual earnings data, and the modeled economic estimate is not an observed personal loss.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official UNICEF Learning Interrupted report page, State of the World's Children context, flagship-report page, and environmental-hazard report page were retrieved; affected-student count, country coverage, lower-income concentration, repeated events, lifetime-earnings estimate, and continuity mechanisms were cross-checked.
